note: Abstract graphs with hand checked answers. `components` lists only the strongly connected components that are cycles: more than one member, or one member with an edge to itself. `minFas` is the size of the smallest set of arcs whose removal makes the whole graph acyclic, worked out by hand. The DAG entries are the negative controls: a detector that reports a cycle in any of them is broken in the way that matters most, because a tool that finds cycles everywhere passes every test that only checks it found the planted one.

graphs.name: single-node
graphs.why: one node, no edges, so it is trivially its own component and not a cycle

graphs.name: dag-diamond
graphs.why: negative control: two paths that rejoin, which a careless reachability check calls a cycle

graphs.name: dag-wide
graphs.why: negative control: 8 nodes, 12 edges, no cycle anywhere

graphs.name: self-loop
graphs.why: a module that imports itself is a cycle of length one

graphs.name: triangle
graphs.why: the case a DFS back edge check reports differently depending on where the walk starts

graphs.name: triangle-with-tails
graphs.why: the same triangle with acyclic nodes hanging off it, which must not join the component

graphs.name: figure-eight
graphs.why: two triangles sharing one node are ONE strongly connected component of five, not two of three

graphs.name: shared-arc
graphs.why: two cycles through the same arc: the minimum is one edge, and a per-cycle greedy answer says two

graphs.name: complete-4
graphs.why: every ordered pair, so every 2-cycle has to lose an arc: six of them

graphs.name: long-chain-then-cycle
graphs.why: a deep acyclic prefix, which is what breaks a recursive Tarjan on a real tree

graphs.name: nested-and-separate
graphs.why: a five node component and a two node component in the same graph, plus a DAG tail
